asparagus-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Asparagus, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Asparagus is the young shoot of a perennial plant of the genus Asparagus. Fresh asparagus is usually steamed, boiled, or grilled without added fat, preserving its natural flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Asparagus is one of the oldest cultivated vegetables, grown for over 2,000 years.
There are three main varieties: green, white (grown in darkness), and purple.
In the United States, asparagus is considered the national spring vegetable.
Only the tender shoots are edible; older spears become woody and fibrous.
Asparagus contains aromatic compounds that give it its distinctive smell.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: 100 g of cooked, fat‑free asparagus provides about 20 kcal, making it an excellent diet food.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate supports DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Asparagus supplies vitamin C, glutathione, and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to asparagus.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Asparagus contains oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: If stored too long or not properly washed, asparagus can become contaminated with bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam, boil for 3‑5 minutes, or quickly grill asparagus without oil. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, omelets, or soups. A pinch of salt and a squeeze of lemon enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep asparagus in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp towel for 3‑5 days. Do not wash before storing to avoid excess moisture.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced Cafe Mocha is a cold beverage made with espresso, milk and chocolate syrup, served over ice. It blends the strength of coffee, the creaminess of milk, and the sweetness of chocolate for a refreshing, aromatic taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first mocha‑latte appeared in the early 1990s in the United States as a chocolate‑flavored variation of the classic latte.
Combining coffee and chocolate enhances perceived bitterness, creating a more balanced drink.
Both dark and milk chocolate syrups are used, altering the intensity of flavor.
Iced Cafe Mocha is often topped with whipped cream and a dusting of cocoa powder.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee and dark chocolate are rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine in espresso increases alertness and concentration.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: The combination of caffeine and theobromine from chocolate can improve mood.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Milk provides calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Coffee contains vitamins B2 and B3, which play roles in energy metabolism.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: High caffeine intake may cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Chocolate syrup and optional sweeteners increase calories and blood sugar levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Milk can cause discomfort for those with lactose intolerance; plant‑based alternatives can be used.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee may aggravate acid reflux in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve Iced Cafe Mocha in tall glasses over ice, garnish with whipped cream and a sprinkle of cocoa. Add vanilla or caramel syrup for flavor variations.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared drink should be kept in the refrigerator and consumed within 24 hours. Store raw ingredients—milk, coffee, and syrup—in their original packaging in a cool, dry place.

content.title: About
content.content: Cookies, Puerto Rican style are a traditional sweet treat made from wheat flour, sugar, eggs, butter, and flavored with cinnamon, cloves, and ground allspice. The dough is rolled into small round discs and baked until golden. They are often enjoyed with tea or coffee and are a staple at festive gatherings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Puerto Rico these cookies are commonly called “polvorones,” which translates to “little crumbs.”
The recipe frequently uses “masacho,” a local cane sugar that gives a distinct caramel note.
Cookies are sometimes dusted with powdered sugar or glazed to mimic the intricate patterns of Puerto Rican pottery.
Some regional variations add raisins or shredded coconut, reflecting Caribbean influences.
They are baked in large batches for family celebrations such as Saint Joseph’s Day and Christmas.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates in the cookies provide quick energy, making them a handy snack before work or study.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Flour and cane sugar contribute a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and butter add vitamins B1, B2, and B6, which aid metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Cinnamon and cloves are rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: Butter supplies monounsaturated fats, which in moderate amounts can be heart‑friendly.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The cookies contain wheat flour, making them unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Butter may cause discomfort for those who cannot digest lactose.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of butter and sugar, the cookies are calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cookies can be enjoyed on their own, paired with hot coffee, tea, or hot chocolate. They also serve as a base for layered cakes, placed between cream layers, or crumbled over ice cream for added texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container at room temperature in a dry place. They can be kept in the refrigerator for up to a week, or frozen for longer storage, retaining flavor for up to three months.

egg-salad-made-with-light-creamy-dressin.title: Egg Salad with Light Creamy Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad with light creamy dressing is a classic 1960s dish made from boiled eggs, a light creamy sauce, herbs, and seasonings. It offers a delicate flavor, a soft texture, and works well as a standalone dish or as a sandwich filling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The recipe gained popularity in post‑war America due to its simplicity and readily available ingredients.
The traditional sauce is made from light mayonnaise, sour cream, and lemon juice, making it less fatty than the classic full‑fat version.
The salad is often served as an appetizer at holiday tables, especially during the summer months.
In the 1960s, advertising campaigns highlighted the salad as a symbol of home comfort and easy home cooking.
Many variations exist, adding mustard, dill, celery, or even avocado for extra flavor.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs supply vitamin B12, riboflavin, and folate, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The light creamy dressing contains less saturated fat than traditional mayonnaise, making the salad more heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, phosphorus, and selenium, important for blood formation and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in the yolk help protect the retina from age‑related changes.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: If eggs are not cooked thoroughly, there is a risk of salmonella contamination.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume the salad in moderation.

items.title: Caloric sauce
items.content: Even a light dressing adds calories; portion control is advisable for those watching their energy intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg salad chilled as an appetizer, as a sandwich filling, in salad bowls, or as a side to vegetable dishes. Garnish with fresh herbs, paprika, or finely diced cucumber for extra color and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Arugula (Eruca vesicaria) is a leafy vegetable with a distinct slightly bitter, nutty flavor. It is cultivated in temperate regions and is commonly used fresh in salads, as a garnish, or in mixed greens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Arugula belongs to the Brassicaceae family, the same as cabbage, broccoli, and mustard.
It was already grown in ancient Rome, where it was prized for its aroma and medicinal properties.
The leaves are rich in glucosinolates, which break down into compounds with potential anti‑cancer effects.
In Italy arugula is often called "rocket" because of the shape of its leaves.
Harvest season is spring and autumn, when the leaves are most tender and flavorful.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Support vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie source of fiber
items.content: Helps regulate digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Glucosinolates and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to arugula.

items.title: Thyroid concerns
items.content: High amounts of glucosinolates can affect thyroid function when consumed in excess.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: As with any fresh produce, wash arugula thoroughly to remove possible bacteria and pesticide residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Arugula is enjoyed raw in salads, tossed with olive oil, lemon juice, nuts, and cheeses. It can also be added to sandwiches, pastas, pizza after baking, or quickly sautéed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store arugula in the refrigerator in a bag or container with a slight moisture layer. Use within 3–5 days. Discard if leaves turn yellow or develop an off odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Pupusa is a traditional Salvadoran dish consisting of a thick corn‑maize tortilla filled with melted cheese. The dough is made from masa (finely ground corn flour) that is cooked to a thick consistency, shaped into a round disc, and then grilled or pan‑fried.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pupusas are often served with curtido (pickled cabbage) and a tomato‑based salsa.
The cheese used is usually a soft, slightly salty variety such as quesillo or mozzarella.
More than 30 regional variations exist in El Salvador, differing in fillings and cooking methods.
Pupusa is considered the national dish of El Salvador and is commonly served at celebrations and family gatherings.
Masa dough is gluten‑free, making pupusas suitable for people with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cheese supplies high‑quality animal protein that supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Cheese contains vitamin B12, important for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Traditional cheese pupusas contain no added sugars, making them suitable for moderate carbohydrate diets.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Masa dough is naturally gluten‑free, safe for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for individuals who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese is often salty, so people monitoring sodium intake should limit portion size.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to milk proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese pupusas are relatively calorie‑dense and should be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pupusas hot, split them open to let the melted cheese ooze out. They are traditionally eaten by hand, accompanied by curtido and salsa. For a lighter option, add fresh vegetables or herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly cooked pupusas are best eaten immediately. If you need to store them, cool them quickly and keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in a skillet or oven to restore a crisp exterior.

content.title: About
content.content: Doritos Nacho Cheese tortilla chips are crunchy corn snacks coated with a savory cheese seasoning. Produced by Frito‑Lay, they are one of the most popular snack foods worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Doritos flavor launched in 1966 was simply "Tortilla," while the Nacho Cheese flavor appeared in 1972.
The seasoning contains milk powder, flavor enhancers, spices and sweeteners, giving the chips their distinctive orange hue.
More than 300 million bags of Doritos are sold each year in the United States alone.
The recipe varies slightly across countries due to local food additive regulations.
Doritos are often used in recipes: as a topping for casseroles, in salsa, or even as a garnish for craft beers.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Corn chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Fiber content
items.content: Corn contains a modest amount of dietary fiber, which supports digestion.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: The cheese seasoning is fortified with calcium and iron, important for bones and blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains vitamins B1, B3 and B6, which aid metabolic processes.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The strong cheese flavor can increase feelings of fullness and help curb overeating.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The seasoning is salty, which may contribute to elevated blood pressure when consumed frequently.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: These chips are high in calories, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: Some batches contain small amounts of trans fats, which are not heart‑healthy.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain milk, soy lecithin and monosodium glutamate—potential allergens for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Doritos can be enjoyed straight from the bag, added to salads, used in Mexican‑style recipes, as a crunchy topping for casseroles, or crushed to coat chicken, fish or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the chips in the original sealed bag, tightly closed after opening, in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer storage, transfer to an airtight container.
